City of Seattle’s Code Complaints and Violations

Aviv Bernstein Livne

Analyzing code violations and enforcement data helps identify frequent built-environment challenges in the city, residents’ concerns/priorities, and the areas with the most frequent challenges. This information can help policymakers improve the built environment, target high-priority concerns, and allocate funding to high-need areas.

To do so, I used the narrative description summaries provided in the City of Seattle’s Code Enforcement Data to classify complaints in the following categories:

  • Neighborhood Blight, which includes abandoned lots, abandoned vehicles, trash, dumping, and demolitions.
  • Vegetation, which includes overgrowth, weeds, and trees.
  • Public Safety, which includes drugs, encampments, illegally occupied units, and police-related issues.
  • Construction, including construction work, unpermitted remodeling, and construction-related disruptions.
  • Noise, which includes noise complaints.
  • Rental Issues, which include tenant/landlord issues.

I created this list of issues based on analyzing the most frequent keywords.

The density plots for each issue over time, beginning in 2003, show that many complaint categories are cyclic. All issues except Rental Issues and Public Safety decrease in the winter. This is likely because vegetation does not grow, construction slows, and people largely stay inside in the winter, resulting in fewer complaints. On the other hand, rental issues likely do not decrease as much in winter because houses can have maintenance issues year-round, and issues related to broken heaters can be very severe.

Tickets are often marked as completed or closed.

The most common last inspection result across all categories was completed though “Compliance Achieved” was also a common outcome.

Focusing on tickets since January 1, 2025, the stacked bar chart below shows that vegetation-related tickets dominate over other ticket types in the summer; however, in the winter, rental issue tickets are most prevalent. Construction, Neighborhood Blight, and Noise see small decreases in the winter relative to other complaint types. November and December 2026 show some tickets in the visualization because a few complaints were inadvertently created for those months, highlighting errors in the dataset. Overall, I am not concerned about the error rates because the dataset is large.

The vast majority of emergency tickets are Rental tickets, while emergencies are not common among other complaint types. There are almost no noise emergencies. While it may seem surprising that few public safety complaints are emergencies, most emergency public safety issues are police matters, not code enforcement matters. Additionally, it may be surprising that there are any vegetation complaints; however, a single complaint can include multiple issues, and if a rental emergency and a vegetation issue appear on the same ticket, the entire ticket is marked as an emergency. Additionally, though uncommon, some vegetation-related emergencies occur, particularly fallen trees that pose safety hazards.

Continuing to analyze data from 2025 and 2026, we see that ticket types are distributed differently throughout the City. Noise and Rental complaints cluster around Belltown, Downtown, Chinatown, Capital Hill, South Lake Union, Ballard, Fremont, and Green Lake. This makes sense because these are some of the busier areas in the City. Public Safety complaints also cluster in these areas, but there are additional clusters in South Seattle. Construction and Neighborhood Blight tickets are fairly uniformly distributed throughout the City. Vegetation tickets are evenly distributed except in the more urban Downtown neighborhoods, essentially the inverse of the Noise complaints.

Emergencies are concentrated in the Capital Hill, Belltown, Downtown, and Ballard neighborhoods.

Stylistic Choices

I chose a density chart to visualize the total ticket volume over time because it shows long-term trends easily. I faceted them by issue and chose an Autumn color palette from Coolors. I used a 1-column, 6-row facet to make the graphs as long as possible, since this data spans a long timeframe and, when it was squished, the trends were impossible to see. I used the same palette for all my visualizations except the heatmaps to keep things consistent and help readers quickly identify the ticket categories, especially since there are 6 categories to track. I used the crest color scheme with a weighted color bar to show ticket status and last inspection results, with a few data entries still visible. I chose a heatmap because it was the only visualization I could think of that would compactly show data from 17 categories across decades. I chose a stacked bar chart to show total ticket volume by category for 2025 and 2026 because it let me quickly compare complaint volume by category. I chose another stacked bar chart for the breakdown of emergency vs. non-emergency complaints for the same reason. I chose a bubble map to show the distribution of complaints by neighborhood because it makes it easy to see which neighborhoods have higher volumes. I chose a choropleth map to show emergencies by neighborhood for the same reason.
